PRELIMINARY STATEMENT 
Petitioner-Plaintiff Moshe Bain (“Bain” or “Petitioner”) respectfully submits this 
memorandum of law in support of his application, via Order to Show Cause, for a temporary 
restraining order and preliminary injunction. Specifically, Petitioner seeks to stay an action 
pending in Supreme Court, Rockland County captioned Strulovitch v. Bleier et al., Index No. 
035405/2024 (the “Rockland Action”), and prevent Respondents-Defendants from taking any 
other actions to confirm and/or enforce an illegal arbitral award. 
Samuel Strulovitch (“Strulovitch”), the primary Respondent-Defendant at bar, initiated the 
Rockland Action to confirm said arbitral award, which purports to grant him partial ownership of 
Parkview Operating Co., LLC , which owns the Westchester Center for Rehabilitation & Nursing 
(hereafter the “Nursing Facility”), and Westchester Gardens Realty LLC, which owns the realty 
on which the Nursing Facility is located (hereafter the “Nursing Facility Property”). But 
Strulovitch improperly excluded Petitioner from both the Rockland Action and from the 
underlying arbitration (which was before a panel of Rockland County Rabbinical Court judges)—
notwithstanding that Petitioner has a documented, uncontested ownership interest in the Nursing 
Facility’s operating and realty companies, and notwithstanding that confirmation of the arbitral 
award would dilute these ownership interests. In so doing, Strulovitch denied Bain procedural and 
substantive due process by deliberately omitting him from the arbitration. 
To remedy that fatal flaw, Petitioner recently initiated his own arbitration before a different, 
Brooklyn-based Rabbinical Court. Unlike Strulovitch, though, Bain joined all the necessary 
parties. At the same time, Bain obtained a remedy akin to a TRO from that Brooklyn-based 
Rabbinical Court precluding Strulovitch from seeking to enforce the award he obtained.

Given the procedural quagmire and due process issues created by Strulovitch, Petitioner 
seeks to stay the Rockland Action (and any other actions Strulovitch might file in an attempt to 
confirm the flawed original Rabbinical Court Award), in order to allow the latest Rabbinical Court 
arbitration to play out. In the alternative, to the extent Strulovitch refuses to participate in the 
arbitration commenced by Bain (which would be contrary to community norms and Strulovitch’s 
own prior invocation of the arbitration process), the Court should stay enforcement of the arbitral 
award pending its adjudication of Baine’s specific performance claim that he has a contractual 
right to acquire any membership interests offered to Strulovitch on account his arbitration award. 
Absent such a stay, Petitioner will be prejudiced because Strulovitch may obtain control of 
membership interests to which he is not entitled on account of Bain’s right of first refusal with 
respect to such interests. 
RELEVANT FACTUAL BACKGROUND1
Beginning in 2010, the parties entered into a series of integrated written agreements under 
which Petitioner and his partners (all of whom are nominal defendants to the action at bar) would 
acquire 100% of the Nursing Facility, a Westchester nursing home, a facility which is highly 
regulated by the New York State Department of Health (“DOH”). Those written agreements 
included an asset purchase agreement (the “APA”), an application to the DOH for approval of the 
transaction, and an assumption of loan agreement, all of which are attached to the Verified PetitionComplaint. The DOH ultimately approved the acquisition. 
Strulovitch was not due to receive any monetary compensation under the APA. He 
therefore communicated to Jonathan Bleier, Petitioner’s primary partner and one of the nominal

Strulovitch then commenced the underlying arbitration before a Rockland County

notwithstanding the fact that Petitioner and others have documented ownership interests in the

The Rockland Action has been assigned to the Hon. Keith Cornell, A.J.S.C. The NYSCEF 
docket reflects that no answering papers have been filed and no discovery has occurred; it further 
reflects that counsel for Strulovitch and Bleier stipulated to an adjournment of the underlying

Petitioner recently asked a different, Brooklyn-based Rabbinical Court to arbitrate the 
dispute over the Nursing Facility and the Nursing Facility Realty, taking into account his 
ownership interests in those entities. Unlike Strulovitch, Petitioner served everyone with asserted 
ownership interests in the Nursing Facility and the Nursing Facility Realty of this pending 
arbitration, including Strulovitch. The Brooklyn Rabbinical Court issued the equivalent of a TRO 
preventing Strulovitch from enforcing the Award until the Brooklyn Rabbinical Court adjudicates 
Petitioner’s claims. (Ex. 14.) The Brooklyn Rabbinical Court further authorized Petitioner to have 
the TRO “certified by the civil courts, so that [Strulovitch] cannot continue there until after [he] 
shall have received a full verdict covering all the partners.” (Id.) 
LEGAL STANDARDS 
Petitioner seeks a preliminary injunction pursuant to CPLR § 7502(c) precluding 
Strulovitch from enforcing the Award pending the outcome of the arbitration commenced by 
Petitioner. To show entitlement to injunctive relief pursuant to CPLR § 7502(c), the party seeking 
the injunction must demonstrate that the arbitral award would be rendered meaningless or 
ineffectual without the granting of the injunction. See, e.g., H.I.G. Capital Mgmt. v. Ligator, 233 
A.D.2d 270 (1st Dep’t 1996); Chiavarelli v. State Univ. of N.Y. Health Sci. Ctr., 248 A.D.2d 712

(2d Dep’t 1998). Critically, the party seeking injunctive relief need not demonstrate irreparable 
harm, a probability of success on the merits and balancing of the equities. See National 
Telecommunications Ass’n, Ltd. v. National Communications Ass’n, Inc., 189 A.D.2d 573 (1st 
Dep’t 1993); see also Guarini v. Severini, 233 A.D.2d 196 (1st Dep’t 1996) (“under CPLR 7502(c) 
the only consideration in deciding whether to grant a preliminary injunction is whether the award 
to which the applicant may be entitled may be rendered ineffectual without such provisional 
relief”); Suffolk Cty. Patrolmen’s Benevolent Ass’n v. County of Suffolk, 150 A.D.2d 361, 361 (2d 
Dep’t 1989) (“CPLR 6301, which governs the grounds for the granting of preliminary injunctions 
and temporary restraining orders, is ‘simply inapplicable’ to applications for injunctive relief in 
such arbitrable controversies”). 
Even if the Court were to find that Petitioner must satisfy the traditional elements to obtain 
injunctive relief, as set forth below, Petitioner can satisfy those elements as well. “The purpose of 
a preliminary injunction is to maintain the status quo and prevent the dissipation of property that 
could render a judgment ineffectual.” Ruiz v. Meloney, 26 A.D.3d 485, 486 (2d Dep’t 2006). 
“The decision to grant or deny a preliminary injunction rests in the sound discretion of the Supreme 
Court.” Id. “Furthermore, even when the facts are in dispute, a court may find a likelihood of 
success on the merits; conclusive proof is not required.” Id. 
A preliminary injunction may be granted in any action where it appears that the 
defendant threatens or is about to do, or is doing or procuring or suffering to be 
done, an act in violation of the plaintiff's rights respecting the subject of the action, 
and tending to render the judgment ineffectual, or in any action where the plaintiff 
has demanded and would be entitled to a judgment restraining the defendant from 
the commission or continuance of an act, which, if committed or continued during 
the pendency of the action, would produce injury to the plaintiff. A temporary 
restraining order may be granted pending a hearing for a preliminary injunction 
where it appears that immediate and irreparable injury, loss or damage will result 
unless the defendant is restrained before the hearing can be had.

CPLR § 6301. “The determination whether to grant a motion for a preliminary injunction rests 
within the sound discretion of the Supreme Court, and requires a party to demonstrate a probability 
of success on the merits, a danger of irreparable injury in the absence of an injunction, and a 
balance of equities in that party’s favor. These elements must be established by clear and 
convincing evidence.” Jones v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Co., 189 A.D.3d 1565, 1566 (2d Dep’t 
2020) (citations omitted).
ARGUMENT 
The Court Should Temporarily Restrain and Preliminarily Enjoin Any Confirmation of 
the Underlying Arbitral Award Until a Full and Fair Proceeding, With All Necessary 
Parties, Can Be Completed by the Rabbinical Court 
I. Absent Injunctive Relief, Any Award Issued to Petitioner Will Be Rendered 
Ineffectual 
As set forth above, in order to obtain a preliminary injunction in aid of arbitration, 
Petitioner need only demonstrate that an arbitration award will be rendered ineffectual absent the 
injunction. See supra. Here, absent a preliminary injunction precluding Strulovitch from 
enforcing the Award, any award obtained by Petitioner will be rendered ineffectual because the 
arbitration commenced by Petitioner challenges the Award. As such, to the extent Petitioner is 
afforded relief in the arbitration he commenced, it will be meaningless if Strulovitch is permitted 
to try and enforce the Award in the interim. Indeed, the Rabbinical Court panel in the arbitration 
commenced by Petitioner recognized that reality, and therefore, the panel issued the equivalent of 
a TRO/injunction precluding Strulovitch from seeking the enforce the Award. (See Ex. 14). This 
Court should do the same and grant Petitioner injunctive relief pending the outcome of the 
arbitration he commenced.

II. Petitioner Also Satisfies the Traditional Preliminary Injunction Elements 
A. Petitioner Has Demonstrated a Likelihood of Ultimate Success on the Merits 
Section 7511(b)(2) of the CPLR states that a challenged arbitral award “shall be vacated 
on the application of a party who neither participated in the arbitration nor was served with a notice 
of intention to arbitrate,” if the court finds that, inter alia, “a valid agreement to arbitrate was not 
made[.]” Here, it is undisputed that Bain did not participate in the original arbitration commenced 
by Strulovitch before the Rockland County Rabbinical Court, and that Strulovitch did not serve 
Bain with notice of said arbitration. The reason for both is obvious; Bain had never agreed to 
arbitrate any dispute regarding ownership of the nursing home. 
The Court need look no further. The language of Section 7511(b)(2) is mandatory, not 
discretionary, and it requires vacatur of an arbitral award where there was no valid agreement to 
arbitrate. Petitioner Bain is thus very likely to ultimately prevail on the merits of his instant Article 
75 action to vacate the original Rabbinical Court Award. 
To the extent the Court wishes to look further, another ground for vacating an arbitral award 
is where the rights of a party were “prejudiced by one of the grounds specified” in Section 
7511(b)(1), e.g., “misconduct in procuring the award” or where an arbitrator “exceeded his power 
or so imperfectly executed it that a final and definite award upon the subject matter submitted was 
not made.” There can be little doubt that Bain’s rights were prejudiced by the challenged Award—
it purports to grant Strulovitch an ownership interest in the Nursing Facility and the Nursing 
Facility Property, which would necessarily dilute Bain’s ownership interests in both of those 
entities. Moreover, the Award simply ignores Bain’s contractual Right of First Refusal. 
Indeed, if it is not vacated, Bain will exercise said right as to any membership interest 
purportedly conveyed to Strulovitch. Under analogous circumstances, Courts have not hesitated

Similarly, there can be little doubt that Strulovitch engaged in “misconduct in procuring 
the award.” Strulovitch deliberately failed to notice Bain about the arbitration—even though he 
knew Bain has an ownership interest in the nursing home—and Strulovitch apparently represented 
to the Rockland County Rabbinical Court that this was a bilateral dispute between himself and 
Bleier. Thus, Bain was unable to assert his interests before the Rockland County Rabbinical Court. 
Moreover, the Rockland County Rabbinical Court so imperfectly executed its power “that 
a final and definite award upon the subject matter submitted was not made.” The Award purports 
to give Strulovitch an ownership stake of 22% in the nursing home—but is utterly silent as to 
anyone else’s ownership stake, including that of Petitioner. Whose ownership interests would be 
diluted, and by how much, in order to grant Strulovitch his purported ownership interest? The 
Award contradicts the contractual agreements that the parties, including Strulovitch himself, had 
signed and been bound to for a decade, and apparently2
 credited Strulovitch’s allegations of a 
secret “side deal” with Bleier—even though Bleier could not unilaterally transfer ownership in the 
nursing home without his partners’ approval. 
Stated differently, by crediting Strulovitch’s claim that he was entitled not only to $1.3 
million in payments over a period of ten years, but also to a substantial ownership stake in the 
nursing home, and then conjuring up a baseless numerical ownership figure of 22%, the challenged

Award in effect rewrote all of the contractual agreements that the parties had signed and been 
bound to for a decade. 
Accordingly, given that Bain did not receive notice of the arbitration commenced by 
Strulovitch, which resulted in the Award that directly implicates Bain’s ownership interests in the 
Nursing Facility and the Nursing Facility Property, the Rockland Action should be stayed and 
Strulovitch should be barred from seeking to enforce the Award. 
B. Danger of Irreparable Injury Absent TRO/Preliminary Injunction 
Strulovitch will inevitably argue that all that is at stake here are the parties’ respective 
ownership interests in the nursing home, which can be monetized and which therefore do not 
qualify as “irreparable injury.” That is false. To the extent Strulovitch obtains an ownership 
interest in the Nursing Facility and Nursing Facility Property, he may also seek to take a role in 
the operation of those businesses. It is well established that interference with a business interest 
is a form of irreparable injury. See David Harp Rest. Mgmt., Inc. v. Cromwell, 183 A.D.2d 423, 
423 (1st Dep’t 1992); Tappan Motors, Inc. v. Waterbury, 318 N.Y.S.2d 125, 126 (Sup. Ct. 
Westchester Cty. 1971). 
Likewise, any claim of ownership by Strulovitch may damage the Nursing Facility’s 
business reputation and goodwill since if he is permitted to continue asserting his ownership claim 
he will cause confusion for the Nursing Facility’s residents and their families, who are dependent 
on clear and accurate information as to who is responsible for their loved ones well-being. It is 
well-established that injury to business reputation and goodwill constitutes irreparable harm and 
merits injunctive relief. See Second on Second Café v. Hing Sing Trading, 66 A.D.3d 255, 272-73 
(1st Dep’t 2009); see also CPTS Hotel Lessee LLC v. Holiday Hosp. Franchising LLC, 171 A.D.3d 
484, 485 (1st Dep’t 2019). That is particularly true in the nursing home context, as the Court of

Appeals has held, “facility operations once compromised for lack of adequate funding may 
occasion irreparable harm within an especially fragile and dependent resident population.” 
Brightonian Nursing Home v. Daines, 21 N.Y.3d 570, 578 (2013). 
Accordingly, Bain faces multiple forms of irreparable harm absent a TRO and preliminary 
injunction precluding Strulovitch from seeking to enforce the Award. 
C. Balance of the Equities 
A balancing of the equities at bar favors the requested TRO/Preliminary Injunction. As an 
initial matter, Petitioner seeks to maintain the status quo—it is Strulovitch who is trying to disrupt 
it by rushing to confirm the original Award via the Rockland Action. Maintaining the status quo 
is of course the very purpose of a preliminary injunction. See Ruiz, 26 A.D.3d at 486; see also 
Johnson v. Johnson, 220 A.D.3d 482, 484 (1st Dep’t 2023) (“balance of the equities favors 
plaintiff, as the Supreme Court stay maintains the status quo”).
 Equally important, Strulovitch acted inequitably by failing to name Bain as a party to the

inconsistent adjudications. See Slifka v. Slifka, 162 A.D.3d 530, 530 (1st Dep’t 2018) (affirming

prevention of inequitable results”); Concord Assoc., L.P. v. EPT Concord, LLC, 101 A.D.3d 1574, 
1575 (3d Dep’t 2012) (“stay would preserve judicial resources, further the interest of justice by 
preventing inequitable results and promote orderly procedure by furthering the goals of comity 
and uniformity” notwithstanding “the parties and issues are not completely identical”).

32. CPLR § 5519(c) gives the court “to which an appeal is taken” discretion to “stay 
all proceedings to enforce the judgment or order appealed from pending an appeal[.]” “In

whether the appeal has merit.” Day v. Plumber’s Shop & Assocs. LLC, 244 N.Y.S.3d 912 (Sup. 
Ct. N.Y. Cnty. 2025) (citations omitted). A court may also consider “the harm that might result to 
the appellant if the stay is denied, and the potential prejudice to the respondent if the stay is

see Da Silva v. Musso, 76 N.Y.2d 436, 443 n.4 (1990) (“the court entertaining the application is 
duty-bound to consider the relative hardships that would result from granting (or denying) a stay”).
